sections.title: 1. Positive feelings toward the captor or abuser
2. Sympathy for the captor's beliefs, behaviors, and goals
3. Negative feelings toward police or other authority figures

toc.title: Thinking it through on the ladder

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory has three brand new additions to the mixed states: intimacy, fawning, and appeasement. Here I'll cover appeasement.

Dr. Porges has a new book, Our Polyvagal World. When I talked with him in my last episode, he spelled out that his son Seth wrote it, and it sounds like Dr. Porges gave it the stamp of approval. The book discusses the application of the Polyvagal Theory to various life domains, like incarceration and schools. But it also adds three new mixed states to the Polyvagal Theory: intimacy, fawn, and appeasement.

Appeasement and fawn are also discussed by Rebecca Bailey, Jaycee Dugard, Stephanie Smith, and Dr. Porges in a paper called "Appeasement: Replacing Stockholm Syndrome as a Definition of a Survival Strategy."

What is appeasement through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory? The basic idea is that appeasement is a sort of co-regulatory mixed state in the face of extreme danger, like a hostage situation. I think the isolation aspect of this is really important.

Through the Polyvagal Theory lens, appeasement is conceptualized as more of a replacement for Stockholm syndrome, and the paper makes it really clear why. We should view appeasement as a two-way neurobiological interaction. The paper calls it a "super social engagement." This is the ability to use social interaction even in these extreme, dangerous situations.

Even though it's called a super social engagement, to me, at least, it seems to be more of a function of de-escalation than actual co-regulation. It's not resulting in the perpetrator becoming more empathetic and compassionate and truly accessing their safe and social state. It seems to be more about de-escalating the potential for harm from the perpetrator.

It also seems to be directly connected to being isolated from others. But maybe there's enough co-regulation happening that it results in de-escalation: neutralizing the perpetrator's defensive state, or neutralizing it enough that significant bodily harm or death is averted.

Appeasement is actually something we see in other mammals as well. I found an article from the Cleveland Clinic on Stockholm syndrome. They use the language of Stockholm syndrome, but they offer one theory for what purpose appeasement might serve: "a learned technique, passed down from our ancestors. In the early civilization, there was always a risk of being captured or killed by another social group. Bonding with captors increases the chance of survival."

So they're postulating it as a learned technique. I think Dr. Porges would say it's more of a biological predisposition to extreme isolation or captivity. I think they're saying something pretty similar, but through different lenses: one sees it as a learned social thing, the other as something ingrained in our DNA as a potential response to extreme situations.
The appeasement paper says that social connection to the perpetrator may be experienced as a type of lifeline. So accessing social connection is directly connected to safety.

When we look at this as a neurobiological interaction between two organisms, we should look at the benefit of connection, even in extreme situations. Mammalian bodies do better when we have more access to our safety state. When our safety state is active, we have more capacity for homeostasis, which is basically using our body's resources for health, growth, and restoration. So simply connecting with somebody, even in a situation like this, may have better results, not just for survival, but for the body's use of its resources and maintaining homeostasis.

So I wouldn't view this as a choice-driven thing. I don't think someone is consciously choosing to connect with their perpetrator. Instead, we want to look at appeasement as a biological drive that optimizes resources.
Dissociation is going to be a factor in appeasement as well, because it helps buffer the understanding of the severity of the situation and its life threat potential.

In other words, existing in a dissociative state is an adaptation that allows that person to not enter a full-on shutdown, which would be life-threatening. Instead of completely shutting down, the body enters a more dissociative, disconnected state that allows basic functioning to continue. The chance of survival increases, but the dissociation keeps that individual from truly recognizing the impact of what they're doing and their connection with the perpetrator.
So this is a mixed state, and the question you're probably asking is: which states are active in the appeasement mixed state? The answer is all of them.

ul: Safety: there is enough activation of the safety state to provide cues of co-regulation to the perpetrator or captor.
Flight and fight: the paper argues the flight and fight state is probably active as well, in order to mobilize and escape if the opportunity arises.

Shutdown: there seems to be a significant amount of dissociation in appeasement, so shutdown is a big part of it too. That dissociation allows for disconnecting from the experience, which means the individual sacrifices their personal values in order to connect with the perpetrator and increase their chances of survival.

blocks.p: I really struggled with understanding appeasement, and fawn, in terms of the Polyvagal Theory and as their own mixed states. But I found an article called "When Agreement Is Not Consent" that really helped me understand what the heck appeasement is and how it connects to the Polyvagal Theory, especially as a biological reaction to distress or extreme situations.

There was a video in that article of a dog appeasing another dog. One dog was the dominant one, and it had this growl to it. As the other dog got close, the dominant dog would growl, and the other dog would roll over onto its back. It was immobile, because it was stiff. But it would also do things like lick the dominant dog's face. So it was submissive. It completely surrendered its power to the other dog, but it also tried to connect and appease it through a social interaction like licking.

When I saw that, I thought: that might be all those states active at once. Immobilized, but also mobilized at the same time, in freeze. And there's some social outreach or social connection going on there, an attempt to show, "Hey, I'm not a threat to you."
There are many potential experiences with appeasement. I'll highlight three of them.

blocks.h3: 1. Positive feelings toward the captor or abuser

blocks.p: I found this quote from Britannica.com on Stockholm syndrome: "Psychologists who have studied the syndrome believe that the bond is initially created when a captor threatens a captive's life, deliberates, and then chooses not to kill the captive. The captive's relief at the removal of the death threat is transposed into feelings of gratitude toward the captor for giving him or her life."

Sadly, I didn't see Britannica give a citation for whoever those psychologists are. So I don't know the exact source. But it makes sense, because the captive is probably connecting their own wellbeing to the "happiness" of their captor, to use that word very loosely.

Remember that our nervous system adapts based on the need for survival. So in order to survive, our nervous system could potentially enter this appeasement state, where we surrender in order to reduce the threat from another. We shouldn't look at this as a choice, exactly. Some people will have the capacity to offer co-regulatory cues to another, but it's really about adapting to the needs of survival.

blocks.h3: 2. Sympathy for the captor's beliefs, behaviors, and goals

blocks.p: The captive identifies that their potential to survive is directly connected to the captor's goals. So it may look like they have sympathy for those goals. The captive learns that compliance and submission to the captor's goals will get their needs met, needs that have otherwise been cut off. Remember, this happens in extreme isolation.

blocks.h3: 3. Negative feelings toward police or other authority figures

blocks.p: These authority figures are a potential threat to the captive's survival, at least while they're in captivity, even though they're supposed to help. In that situation, in isolation, under duress and life threat, the captive is now in agreement, in a sense, with the captor on their goals, and views others as dangerous. The captive's needs for survival are being met by the captor, and appeasement is a major way of continuing to get those needs met.
Again, don't look at this as them choosing this, or liking being part of this type of relationship.

blocks.h: Thinking it through on the ladder

blocks.p: Think of it in terms of the polyvagal ladder. The captive cannot connect with the other person in a very meaningful, safe and social way, but they can do so enough to reduce threat. They can't really run away. They can't really fight. They've been isolated and trapped. They also can't exist in a shutdown state for very long, because that would result in death.

So the captive, as a mammal, is using their best means of getting their needs met and surviving. That's existing in a dissociative state that allows them to stay mobilized to run away if they can, and also allows them to surrender their own personal values and connect with the captor convincingly enough, through co-regulatory cues, to reduce the captor's defenses.

And if you think about it that way, the potential for escape probably goes up. I don't know stats on how often this is effective. But from the biological interaction between captor and captive, through this neuroception of co-regulation, or even pseudo co-regulation, I think there's probably more of a chance of escape if the captor reduces their defensive or aggressive state. If the captor is less defensive or less aggressive, there may be some sort of pseudo trust, some space given to the person that allows them to get out of the situation.
